title: Behar: proclaim liberty (Leviticus 25:8–10)
hook: in the fiftieth year, "proclaim liberty throughout the land"

segments.voice: Yesterday, shmita: every seventh year the land rests. Your line was the land rests too. Did you leave something unworked? Today, what happens after seven of those sevens. Day four hundred twenty-one.

In Philadelphia there's a cracked bell that people line up to see. Around its crown runs an inscription, with a chapter and verse beside it: proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof. It was cast in the 1750s for the Pennsylvania State House. Later, abolitionists adopted it and gave it the name it carries now, the Liberty Bell. The words on it were already ancient. They come from Leviticus 25, and from a year the Torah calls the yovel.
screen: `A CRACKED BELL IN PHILADELPHIA.` → `THE WORDS AROUND ITS CROWN.` → `LEVITICUS 25.`

segments.voice: First, the count. Seven sabbatical years, seven times seven, forty-nine years. Then, on Yom Kippur of the next year, the shofar sounds through the whole land. Second, the proclamation. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land unto all the inhabitants thereof; it shall be a jubilee unto you". Land that was sold goes back to the family that held it. Israelites who sold themselves into service go free, home to their families. Every fifty years, the board resets. Third, the words. Yovel is the ram's horn; the Talmud says that in Arabia they called a ram yovla. The year is named for the sound that announces it. Through Latin, yovel became our English jubilee. And the word for liberty, deror, Rashi explains as the freedom to live wherever you wish, not under someone else's control. Some link it to a bird, the deror, that nests freely wherever it likes. Fourth, honesty about history. The Talmud says the jubilee was kept only while all the tribes lived on their land, and stopped once they were exiled. Whether it was ever fully practiced is debated, and the sources are thin. But the idea outlived the practice: that land and people aren't meant to be owned forever, that debts and losses shouldn't pass down without end. A bell in Philadelphia carries the words still.
screen: `SEVEN TIMES SEVEN YEARS.` · `LAND RETURNS, PEOPLE GO HOME.` · `YOVEL: THE RAM'S HORN.` · `KEPT ONLY WHILE THE TRIBES WERE HOME.` · then, large: `PROCLAIM LIBERTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: free someone from an old debt. Settle, and breathe. Think of something someone owes you. Money, maybe. Or an apology you've been waiting on for years, a favor never returned, a debt of attention. Ask whether it's time for a jubilee. Not because they've earned it. Because fifty years is long enough, or five. Picture telling them, or just deciding inside: you owe me nothing for this anymore. Notice what changes when the debt is gone. The bell holds the time.
Yovel. The jubilee: the fiftieth year, announced by the ram's horn, when land returns, people go free, and liberty is proclaimed throughout the land.
Your line: proclaim liberty. Today, release one person from something they owe you, and tell them if you can. Day four hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: The jubilee is not observed today; rabbinic law holds it lapsed when the tribes were exiled. Jews read Behar in synagogue each year, and the jubilee's ideal of release is often cited in Jewish teaching on debt and freedom.

notes: JPS 1917 Lev 25:10 quoted from memory; confirm wording, especially 'hallow' and 'jubilee unto you'.

The Liberty Bell inscription follows the KJV ('Proclaim LIBERTY throughout all the Land unto all the Inhabitants thereof'); the hook gives it in lowercase without quotation marks. Cast 1752–53 for the Pennsylvania State House; the name 'Liberty Bell' came from abolitionists in the 1830s. Confirm.
Rosh Hashanah 26a: Rabbi Akiva heard 'yovla' for a ram in Arabia; confirm.
Rashi on 25:10 (from Rosh Hashanah 9b): deror as dwelling wherever one wishes; the bird (dror) link is a traditional explanation. Confirm.
Arakhin 32b: jubilee observed only when all tribes dwell on their land; confirm. Historical practice is debated; the script says so.
Hook softened from 'more than two thousand years old' to 'already ancient', since the dating of Leviticus is debated among scholars.
'Yovel became our English jubilee through Latin' (iubilaeus, influenced by iubilare): confirm.

Editor review (y2 judaism 407–425): cut the unsourced 'millions' and the claim that most visitors don't know the source (the bell itself cites Lev. XXV); 'notice how it feels' reworded so the listener isn't told a feeling.
